newCitations.caseName: American General Life Insurance Company, et al. v. 500-512 Seventh Avenue Limited Partnership (Chetrit/Moinian/Minskoff Garment District Building)
newCitations.citation: Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County (foreclosure order entered August 2026)
newCitations.outcome: AIG-affiliated lenders (American General Life, Variable Annuity Life, United States Life) sued to foreclose on the $375M loan taken against the leasehold in 2018, alleging intentional self-dealing and diversion of funds by the Chetrit/Moinian/Minskoff ownership group. Facing a debt that had grown to roughly $356M with accrued interest and fees, the borrower agreed not to oppose the lender's foreclosure motion, and the court ordered the buildings sent to a foreclosure auction to satisfy the debt.
newCitations.notes: Borrower's decision not to oppose foreclosure despite live self-dealing allegations is itself a data point: even where a lender's complaint alleges borrower misconduct, an undisputed-default posture can still resolve as a clean, uncontested foreclosure once the numbers are hopeless. Also illustrates a garment-district office tower where original 1999 leasehold acquisition cost ($140M) was far below the 2018 loan amount ($375M), i.e., significant equity extraction well before the default.

newCitations.caseName: Ocean West Capital Partners / Daol Asset Management (on behalf of a consortium of South Korean insurers) v. RFR Realty (285 Madison Avenue)
newCitations.citation: UCC Article 9 public foreclosure auction of pledged mezzanine equity interests, held April 15, 2025 at DLA Piper LLP offices, New York (and via Zoom)
newCitations.outcome: The $205M mezzanine loan on RFR's 511,000-square-foot Midtown Manhattan office tower fell into maturity default in late 2022; an extension bought time but the loan defaulted again in late 2024 when that extension expired. The mezzanine lender consortium (advised by Ocean West Capital Partners and Daol Asset Management) foreclosed non-judicially under UCC Article 9 on the pledged LLC equity interests rather than proceeding through a judicial mortgage foreclosure, and took ownership of the property at the April 2025 auction, wiping out RFR's equity with no reported cash deficiency recovery pursued against RFR beyond the loss of the collateral itself.
newCitations.notes: A mezzanine UCC Article 9 foreclosure is legally distinct from a mortgage foreclosure/deficiency judgment (it forecloses on pledged personal property -- equity interests -- not the real property itself, and is typically non-judicial and much faster), but produces the same economic result for the borrower: total loss of the asset with no further deficiency exposure beyond the mezz collateral. Relevant to calibrating this claim type wherever the fact pattern involves mezzanine rather than senior mortgage debt, which is now common in stacked CRE capital structures.

newCitations.caseName: Rhinebeck Bank v. WA 319 Main, LLC
newCitations.outcome: After the collateral sold at foreclosure auction for $795,001 against a judgment of roughly $1.16M, the trial court calculated the deficiency using the lender's appraiser's lower 'liquidation value' ($620,000) rather than fair market value, awarding a larger deficiency. The Second Department reversed, holding fair market value (found to be approximately $1.06M) is the correct benchmark under RPAPL 1371, not a discounted liquidation value -- which, because $1.06M exceeded the auction price, sharply reduced the deficiency judgment to $104,186.56.
newCitations.notes: A real, recent example of a lender winning the foreclosure/deficiency claim in principle but recovering far less than sought because of a valuation methodology fight -- useful even where the default itself is undisputed, since the deficiency AMOUNT (not just the right to one) can be knocked down substantially on appeal when a liquidation-value appraisal is used instead of fair market value.

newCitations.caseName: Lifestyle Real Estate Lender, LLC v. Fred Rappaport, et al.
newCitations.outcome: After the lender purchased the collateral for a nominal $1,191.55 at a July 2018 Pennsylvania sheriff's sale following the underlying mortgage foreclosure (which had produced a roughly $4.9M judgment), the lender sued the guarantors in federal court to collect that judgment amount under the guaranty via breach-of-contract and unjust-enrichment theories. The court held that Pennsylvania's Deficiency Judgment Act did not govern the action because the only Pennsylvania connection was the pledged (vacant) collateral, and expressly declined to resolve the guarantors' ultimate contractual liability for the ~$4.9M on that motion, leaving the merits of guarantor liability for further proceedings rather than deciding it outright.
newCitations.notes: Illustrates a real procedural trap distinct from the substantive availability-of-deficiency issue already modeled in foreclosureStateModifiers: which state's deficiency-judgment statute (if any) even applies can itself be contested and require its own choice-of-law-style analysis, independent of the merits of the underlying debt. Outcome on guarantor liability itself was not fully resolved as of this research pass -- confidence marked medium because only the procedural ruling, not a final merits disposition, was confirmed.

foreclosure_deficiency_judgment.calibrationNote: The expanded sample still supports the existing 0.85-0.97 base range for undisputed defaults: three of four new citations (500-512 Seventh Avenue, 285 Madison Avenue, and the underlying Rhinebeck Bank sheriff's sale) are clean lender wins on the right to collect. But Rhinebeck Bank is a useful refinement to the DAMAGES side rather than the probability side: even with an uncontested default, the deficiency AMOUNT can swing substantially (there, cut by roughly 90% on appeal) depending on whether fair-market-value or liquidation-value appraisal methodology is used -- worth a note in the damages formula alongside the existing lender-protective-advances point. The Lifestyle Real Estate Lender case is a reminder that state deficiency-judgment-statute APPLICABILITY itself can be litigated as a threshold question distinct from the state-specific availability rules already captured in foreclosureStateModifiers.

newCitations.caseName: Brick Air Capital LLC v. NLD Props., Inc.
newCitations.citation: Index No. 850613/2023 (N.Y. Sup. Ct., N.Y. Cnty.), order dated October 11, 2024
newCitations.outcome: In a commercial mortgage foreclosure action over property at 2310 Second Avenue in Manhattan, the plaintiff-lender moved for appointment of a receiver, relying on a consent-to-receivership clause in the mortgage. The court denied the motion, holding that under New York Real Property Law Sec. 254(10) a receiver-consent clause makes appointment proper without notice or regard to the sufficiency of the security, but does not make appointment automatic -- the court retains equitable discretion to deny it even where the parties contractually agreed to it. A referee was appointed instead to compute the amount due and assess whether the property could be sold in parcels.
newCitations.notes: A clean, recent example of a receivership motion being DENIED even with a contractual consent-to-receiver clause in hand -- a useful counterweight to this claim type's currently grant-heavy sample, and doctrinally distinct from the Adelaide Pointe pattern (there, the issue was factual disputes; here, the court exercised pure equitable discretion despite no apparent dispute about default).

newCitations.caseName: Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (Freddie Mac) v. VE Lakeview LP
newCitations.citation: U.S. District Court, Middle District of Georgia, Macon Division, filed June 30, 2026
newCitations.outcome: Freddie Mac sued to appoint a receiver over Lakeview Apartments, a 96-unit Fort Valley, Georgia multifamily property, after the borrower made no monthly payment on its $2,564,000 loan since February 1, 2025. The lender invoked a consent-to-receiver clause in the security instrument (agreed in advance, requiring no separate notice) and cited a 2025 HUD inspection finding 'significant and life-threatening issues' at the property. As of this research, no ruling on the receivership motion had been reported.
newCitations.notes: Smaller-balance loan than most of this claim type's sample (~$2.56M vs. the eight/nine-figure office towers dominating the file), showing the fact pattern -- payment default plus a life-safety/habitability angle -- also recurs at the smaller end of the multifamily market, not just trophy office assets.

newCitations.caseName: Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. (as Trustee, by and through KeyBank National Association as Special Servicer and Attorney-in-Fact) v. Workspace Property Trust (portfolio entities)
newCitations.citation: Maricopa County Superior Court, Arizona, filed September 2025
newCitations.outcome: The lender sued to foreclose on a CMBS-securitized loan portfolio of 143 suburban office/flex properties across Arizona, Florida, Minnesota, and Pennsylvania, with an unpaid principal balance of roughly $1.23 billion (down from a $1.63 billion issuance value per Morningstar Credit) against a portfolio that had fallen from about 89% occupancy at origination to roughly 75%. Trigild was appointed receiver over the entire portfolio pending resolution of the foreclosure.
newCitations.notes: By far the largest-dollar receivership in this claim type's sample and a useful data point on multi-state, multi-property portfolio receiverships (as opposed to single-asset receiverships, which make up the rest of the sample) -- occupancy decline from ~89% to ~75% over the loan's life is a similar distress signature to the office-sector fact pattern already noted for this claim type.

newCitations.caseName: Independent Bank v. Adelaide Pointe Boaters Services, LLC, et al.
newCitations.citation: Kent County (Mich.) Circuit Court, Business Court, Case No. 17-2025-20760-CBB, opinion dated January 9, 2026
newCitations.outcome: On the bank's renewed motion following development of the factual record, the Business Court held Independent Bank entitled to appointment of a receiver over the mixed-use marina/boat-services development under Michigan's Assignment of Rents Act, on more than $28 million in construction loans in default. The court held that where the assignor is in default and the underlying mortgage authorizes a receiver upon default, the statutory requirement is satisfied even absent a separate receiver clause in the rent assignment itself, and proceeded to select a receiver after considering the parties' competing nominees.
newCitations.notes: This is the final resolution of the SAME case already referenced in this claim type's existing note ('the lone initial denial, Independent Bank v. Adelaide Pointe, was later granted on renewed motion once factual disputes were developed') -- included here as a full citation because the existing file only mentioned it in a narrative note, without a citation entry giving the actual holding, dollar amount, and doctrinal basis (Assignment of Rents Act satisfied by a receiver-on-default clause in the mortgage, even without a matching clause in the rent assignment).

newCitations.caseName: In re receivership of a downtown St. Louis hotel (lender v. hotel ownership entity)
newCitations.citation: Missouri state court (St. Louis City Circuit Court), receiver appointed April 30, 2026
newCitations.outcome: A Missouri state judge appointed a receiver over a downtown St. Louis hotel following a $35 million loan default, with the receiver expected to keep the hotel operating while filing an operating plan and periodic reports with the court.
newCitations.notes: Confidence marked low because the source article did not name the specific hotel, borrower, lender, or case/docket number -- the loan amount, jurisdiction, and outcome (receiver appointed) are reported, but this citation cannot be independently verified against a primary court record the way the others in this set can. Included only as a directional data point that receivership activity in the current distress cycle extends to hospitality assets, not just office and multifamily.

receivership_dispute.calibrationNote: The expanded sample (9 cases total counting the original 6-case set) still shows receivers granted more often than not, but the new citations meaningfully diversify the small original sample: Brick Air Capital is a second clean DENIAL (distinct from the already-noted Adelaide Pointe fact-dispute denial) resting purely on a court's equitable discretion even where the mortgage's consent-to-receiver clause was satisfied on its face. That is real evidence the 0.65-0.85 range should not be pushed toward its upper bound as a default assumption, and perhaps argues for treating 'has a consent-to-receiver clause' as necessary-but-not-sufficient rather than as a near-certain predictor the way this claim type's note currently implies. The Workspace Property Trust and Adelaide Pointe citations also show the fact pattern is not limited to distressed-office-tower single assets -- large multi-state portfolios and construction-loan/marina developments both fit the same doctrinal analysis.

newCitations.caseName: 172 Madison (NY) LLC v. NMP-Group, LLC, et al.
newCitations.citation: Index No. 650087/2010 (N.Y. Sup. Ct., N.Y. Cnty., Commercial Div.)
newCitations.outcome: UBS Securities made a $29 million non-recourse loan in 2007 secured by Midtown Manhattan real property; the borrower's principal executed a standard non-recourse carve-out guaranty. After the borrower defaulted and the lender commenced a foreclosure action including a guaranty claim, the borrower later filed for bankruptcy. The court held that the voluntary bankruptcy filing triggered the guaranty's full-recourse springing provision, entitling the lender to seek immediate full repayment from the guarantor notwithstanding New York's 'one action' rule, which normally would have required the lender to exhaust the mortgaged property first.
newCitations.notes: A bankruptcy-filing trigger case (rather than the SPE-insolvency-covenant trigger common to the Cherryland/Gratiot Avenue line already in the file), and notable for holding the springing guaranty enforceable even against New York's normally borrower-protective 'one action' rule.

newCitations.caseName: Bank Mutual v. S.J. Boyer Construction, Inc.
newCitations.outcome: After the mortgaged properties sold at sheriff's sale for $1,180,000 against roughly $1.4 million owed, the bank elected a shortened statutory redemption period, which under Wisconsin law waives any deficiency claim against the BORROWER. The Wisconsin Supreme Court held that election does not also waive the lender's separate claim against the GUARANTOR, because guarantor liability arises under an entirely separate contract of guaranty rather than from the mortgage debt itself -- allowing the bank to obtain judgment against the guarantor for the full guaranteed debt even after forfeiting a deficiency claim against the primary obligor.
newCitations.notes: A strong pro-lender landmark on a distinct doctrinal point from the existing sample: a guaranty is legally independent of the underlying mortgage debt, so procedural elections that extinguish a borrower's deficiency exposure (redemption-period elections, anti-deficiency statutes, etc.) do not automatically protect a guarantor unless the guaranty itself says so.

newCitations.caseName: Borman, LLC v. Borman, LLC; Joseph Schwebel
newCitations.outcome: A purchaser standing in the original lender's shoes sued the borrower and guarantor Joseph Schwebel to collect a roughly $6 million deficiency, relying on a solvency covenant in the guaranty as the full-recourse trigger. The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment FOR the guarantor, holding that Michigan's post-Cherryland Nonrecourse Mortgage Loan Act (NMLA) rendered the solvency covenant unenforceable and therefore barred the deficiency action entirely -- the guarantor owed nothing on the $6 million claim.
newCitations.notes: A direct, important counterweight to Cherryland and Gratiot Avenue (both already in the file, both pre-NMLA and both full guarantor losses on the same insolvency-covenant theory): this case shows Michigan's 2011 legislative fix actually working in a guarantor's favor to defeat an otherwise-identical full-recourse claim. Confirms that jurisdiction and TIMING relative to a state's legislative response matters enormously for this claim type -- a state-law modifier tracking which states have passed anti-full-recourse statutes (Michigan, and per the existing file's note, Ohio) would likely sharpen this claim type more than a flat national probability range does.

newCitations.caseName: Lifestyle Real Estate Lender, LLC v. Fred Rappaport, et al.
newCitations.outcome: Lender sued guarantors Dr. Rappaport and an estate to collect a roughly $4.9 million judgment already entered in the underlying mortgage foreclosure, via breach-of-contract and unjust-enrichment claims under the guaranty (the lender had already taken the collateral at a nominal sheriff's sale price). The court held Pennsylvania's Deficiency Judgment Act did not apply to the action because the property's only Pennsylvania connection was the pledged vacant collateral, and expressly reserved the question of the guarantors' ultimate contractual liability for further proceedings rather than resolving it on this motion.
newCitations.notes: Same underlying case as the citation added to foreclosure_deficiency_judgment -- included here too because it bears directly on guaranty enforcement mechanics: which state's deficiency-judgment framework (if any) governs a guaranty-collection suit can itself become a contested threshold question, independent of the guaranty's substantive terms. Confidence marked medium because the final merits ruling on guarantor liability was not confirmed.

guaranty_enforcement.calibrationNote: The expanded sample sharpens rather than undermines the existing 0.7-0.92 base range, but suggests the range is really tracking TWO different populations that happen to average out similarly: (1) SPE-covenant/bankruptcy-trigger cases in states with no legislative carve-back (172 Madison, and the file's existing Cherryland/Princeton Park/Gratiot Avenue) plus the independent-contract doctrine reinforcing lender remedies (Bank Mutual), where guarantors lose close to automatically once a trigger is credibly alleged -- consistent with the current high end; versus (2) the same fact pattern in a state with a post-Cherryland statutory fix, where Borman shows the guarantor can win outright and owe nothing on an identical theory. Because Michigan and Ohio specifically passed anti-full-recourse statutes in response to Cherryland, this claim type would benefit from a state-law modifier (similar to foreclosureStateModifiers) flagging those two states as guarantor-favorable outliers, rather than relying on the flat national range to implicitly average over a jurisdictional split this stark.

newCitations.caseName: Credit Suisse AG, Cayman Islands Branch v. Claymore Holdings, LLC
newCitations.citation: No. 18-0403 (Tex. Apr. 24, 2020); on remand, No. 05-21-00649-CV (Tex. App.-Dallas Feb. 14, 2023)
newCitations.outcome: Claymore (an affiliate of Highland Capital Management) alleged Credit Suisse, which arranged a $250 million tranche of $540 million in loans refinancing a Henderson, Nevada residential development, fraudulently inflated the underlying appraisal to induce Claymore's participation. A jury awarded $40 million in fraud damages and a separate bench trial added $211 million in equitable rescissory damages plus a further ~$23 million for Claymore's secondary-market purchases. The Texas Supreme Court affirmed the $40 million fraud verdict in 2020 but reversed the $211 million rescissory award as duplicative of an adequate legal remedy. On remand, the Dallas Court of Appeals in 2023 went further, vacating the $23 million secondary-market award entirely and reducing the $40 million fraud verdict itself to a take-nothing judgment after crediting Credit Suisse for settlements Claymore had already reached with other co-liable tortfeasors -- leaving Claymore with a net recovery of zero after roughly a decade of litigation.
newCitations.notes: Not a borrower-vs-originating-lender dispute like most of this claim type's sample -- Claymore was itself a sophisticated institutional CRE lender/investor suing an arranging bank for fraud in how a loan was marketed/appraised, a distinct but real lender-liability-adjacent theory relevant to syndicated/participated CRE debt. The arc from a combined $274M in trial awards down to zero is a vivid, well-documented illustration of appellate erosion risk even after a plaintiff wins outright at trial on a lender-misconduct theory -- directly relevant to calibrating the damages formula's realistic expected value, not just the probability of an initial finding of liability.

newCitations.caseName: WWP Mezz LLC v. WWP Mezz Investment Company LLC (Worldwide Plaza)
newCitations.citation: Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County, Commercial Division, decision dated January 27, 2026
newCitations.outcome: SL Green (indirect owner of the mezzanine borrower at Worldwide Plaza) sought a preliminary injunction to block a UCC Article 9 sale of the pledged equity interests after a mezzanine loan default, arguing the sale terms (including 'Qualified Bidder' requirements) were commercially unreasonable and that the lender's conduct violated the implied covenant of good faith. Justice Andrea Masley denied the preliminary injunction, holding the proposed sale terms were commercially reasonable under UCC Sec. 9-610(b) and rejecting the borrower-side challenge, allowing the sale to proceed as scheduled.
newCitations.notes: Directly comparable to the 111 West 57th/Steinway Tower citation already in the file (same theory -- a lender's contractual discretion in a mezzanine-loan enforcement context challenged as bad-faith/commercially unreasonable) but with the OPPOSITE outcome: here the borrower-side challenge was rejected outright at the injunction stage rather than reinstated on appeal, underscoring how fact-specific and procedurally contingent (preliminary injunction vs. post-dismissal appeal) these outcomes are.

newCitations.caseName: 601W Companies (Civic Opera House / 20 N. Wacker Drive) v. Rialto Capital Advisors
newCitations.citation: Counterclaim filed in CMBS special-servicer foreclosure action, Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, filed May 31, 2024
newCitations.outcome: After the underlying $164 million loan (with accrued interest and fees exceeding $195 million) on Chicago's Civic Opera House building went into pandemic-era default, borrower 601W alleged it proactively sought a workout, but special servicer Rialto Capital negotiated in bad faith and made repeated unreasonable refusals of proposed solutions, filing a counterclaim describing Rialto's special-servicing conduct as 'predatory.' As of this research, no ruling on the counterclaim's merits had been reported.
newCitations.notes: One of a documented wave of CMBS-borrower counterclaims against special servicers (Rialto in particular) emerging from the 2023-2025 office distress cycle -- useful alongside the already-cited ROC Debt Strategies case to show this fact pattern (special-servicer-as-defendant rather than originating-lender-as-defendant) recurring across multiple, unrelated properties and courts.

newCitations.caseName: Midtown Equities (Joseph Cayre) v. Rialto Capital Advisors / Blackstone (205 Montague Street, Brooklyn Heights)
newCitations.citation: Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County, filed February 25, 2025; dismissed with prejudice March 2025
newCitations.outcome: Midtown Equities filed a putative class action alleging Rialto (as special servicer on a $45 million Signature Bank-originated loan) and Blackstone engaged in a 'campaign of deception' to manufacture a default and coerce the borrower into paying default interest and fees rather than granting a routine loan extension. Ten days after filing, the parties reached a settlement, and the lawsuit was dismissed with prejudice in March 2025.
newCitations.notes: A fast-settled, dismissed-with-prejudice outcome from the same current wave of CMBS-servicer lender-liability suits as the 601W/Rialto and ROC Debt Strategies citations -- illustrates that these theories, even when filed as headline-grabbing class actions with aggressive 'predatory'/'deception' framing, often resolve quickly and confidentially rather than through adjudicated wins. Confidence marked medium because the settlement's terms (and thus whether Midtown recovered anything of value) were not disclosed.

lender_liability_claim.calibrationNote: The expanded sample reinforces keeping the base probability at the LOW end of the existing 0.15-0.35 (non-egregious) range, if anything more strongly than before: of the outcomes that could actually be confirmed, borrower/plaintiff lender-liability theories lost or were rejected across the board in the current cycle -- WWP Mezz's injunction was denied outright, Midtown Equities' claims were dismissed with prejudice (albeit after a quick settlement), and even Claymore Holdings' rare full trial win against Credit Suisse was whittled down to zero on appeal via settlement credits after nearly a decade of litigation. Only the still-pending 601W/Rialto counterclaim keeps the door open for a borrower-side win in this specific sample. This is consistent with the file's existing note that recent CRE lender-liability suits are 'trending toward procedural wins... rather than dollar outcomes,' and arguably supports lowering the top of the non-egregious range slightly rather than leaving it at 0.35.
